R1.rule: Make each class and method either an Integration or an Operation, never both.

R8.rule: Cover Operations with focused unit tests.

R9.rule: Cover Integrations with a small number of integration or wiring tests.

R10.rule: Write the simplest code that solves the current, actual problem.

R11.rule: Do not add abstractions, generics, or extension points for hypothetical future requirements.

R12.rule: Do not design for reusability when something is used in only one place.

R13.rule: Do not make things configurable when a constant works for now.

R14.rule: Do not add parameters, interfaces, or indirection that serve no present purpose.

R15.rule: Make domain logic functionally pure: same inputs produce same outputs with no side effects.

R16.rule: Do not make domain logic depend on I/O, file access, network calls, UI interaction, or uninjected randomness or time.

R17.rule: Isolate I/O concerns at the edges of the system.

R18.rule: When domain logic needs an external value such as the current time, inject it as a parameter instead of reading it inside the logic.

R19.rule: Do not mix domain logic and I/O concerns.

R22.rule: The no-inline-construction rule does not apply to test code.

R23.rule: Use comments sparingly, if at all.

R24.rule: Put the reasoning behind a decision in the git commit message, not in code comments.

R25.rule: When a comment feels needed, first rename the method, class, or variable so the name carries that meaning.

R26.rule: Write a comment only if no name can express the meaning.

R27.rule: Do not write doc-block summaries that restate a well-named function's behavior.

R28.rule: Do not write module-header prose explaining the domain.

R39.rule: Do not re-validate what the framework already ensures.

R40.rule: Prefer letting unexpected failures propagate and crash loudly (fail-fast) rather than silently swallowing them with defensive code.
